sections.section_title: 1. Clinical Presentation and Rapid Recognition of Multiphase Anaphylaxis
sections.description: This section outlines the initial signs and symptoms that triggered emergency care, details the timeline of symptom onset, and explains how clinicians distinguish a classic anaphylactic crisis from potential biphasic or multiphasic patterns early in the ED workflow.
subtopics: Patient demographics and relevant comorbidities
Initial trigger (clarithromycin) and timing of symptom onset
Key anaphylaxis signs: hypotension, hypoxaemia, urticaria, flushing, pruritus, angio‑like edema
Differential assessment of airway compromise vs. systemic shock
Immediate criteria for diagnosing anaphylaxis (AAACI/FAAN)
Recognising early warning signs of biphasic recurrence (i.e., symptom resolution followed by relapse)

sections.section_title: 2. Standard Emergency Management of Anaphylaxis and Adaptation to Multiphasic Course
sections.description: This part explains the evidence‑based initial resuscitation steps for anaphylaxis, the pharmacologic rationale for epinephrine dosing and adjuncts, and discusses the special challenges posed by a patient who relapses multiple times despite adequate initial therapy.
subtopics: Epinephrine pharmacodynamics and dose‑weight relationships
Choice of auto‑injector (0.3 mg vs 0.5 mg) and dosing implications in >50‑kg adults
Use of intramuscular vs intravenous routes
Adjunctive therapies: antihistamines, corticosteroids (historical role vs recent evidence), fluid resuscitation
Assessment of response and criteria for escalation
Monitoring for emerging biphasic/multiphasic episodes (time window, clinical vigilance)

sections.section_title: 3. Diagnostic Work‑up of Recurrent Anaphylaxis and Identification of Underlying Predisposition
sections.description: Here we describe the laboratory and imaging investigations undertaken once the multiphasic pattern was recognised, focusing on measuring serum tryptase, evaluating for systemic mastocytosis, and the limitations of current diagnostic criteria in this setting.
subtopics: Serial tryptase sampling protocol (time points, interpretation of peak and baseline values)
WHO diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis – major/minor findings
Bone marrow biopsy considerations and limitations
Imaging findings: hepatomegaly, other organ involvement
Clinical manifestations supporting mast cell disease (depression, memory issues)
Risk stratification based on underlying mast cell disorders

sections.section_title: 4. Management Strategies for Biphasic and Multiphasic Anaphylaxis – Evidence, Gaps, and Practical Guidance
sections.description: This section critically evaluates current guideline recommendations for observation duration, corticosteroid use, and anticipatory therapy (continuous epinephrine infusion vs. expectancy), highlighting evidence gaps and proposing a reasoned approach to care in similar cases.
subtopics: Guideline consensus on observation periods (UK, NHG, WAO) and risk‑stratified models
Corticosteroid efficacy: systematic review data vs. practice patterns
Continuous epinephrine infusion: indications, risks, monitoring needs
Expectant approach: monitoring to 24–48 h, when to intervene
Resource allocation: ICU vs. ward care for multiphasic patients
Future research priorities and registry development

sections.section_title: 5. Clinical Outcomes, Follow‑up, and Patient Education
sections.description: The final section covers the post‑acute management, including hospital discharge planning, patient education on self‑administration of epinephrine, prophylactic antihistamine therapy, and long‑term surveillance for underlying mast cell disease.
subtopics: Criteria for transition from ICU to general ward and discharge
Long‑term antihistamine strategy (levocetirizine) and rationale
Education on epinephrine auto‑injector use and dosage compliance
Follow‑up schedule for tryptase monitoring and symptom assessment
Counselling on allergen avoidance and psychological support
Re‑evaluation for definitive diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis
